Thank you very much, Your Excellency, for your statement and the pledge. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Olav Myklebust, Ambassador of Norway to the United Nations, Arab Emirates. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, good morning, all. I would like to begin by expressing our sincere appreciation to the United Arab Emirates for hosting the 15th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice. chairing the negotiations of the Abu Dhabi Declaration, collecting evidence across borders, identifying proceeds of crime abroad, securing and confiscating such assets, and holding enablers accountable. We must also take the necessary steps to ensure that UNODC is positioned to effectively exercise its mandate. President, A key theme of the Crime Congress is how to strengthen crime prevention, address new forms of crime, and promote people-centred justice systems. Combating child and youth crime must therefore be a priority. In Norway, youth crime has declined overall, but offenders are becoming younger and are committing more serious crimes, often linked to criminal networks. Social media and digital platforms allow criminal networks to recruit vulnerable children and young people by offering money, status and a sense of belonging. Violence is organised online, while algorithms and gaming-related references can help normalise criminal activity. This trend is deeply concerning. Norway does not want to respond primarily with harsher punishment for youth offenders, but with stronger prevention and early intervention. Prevention requires timely and coordinated efforts across sectors. The government has introduced several measures, including one-to-one follow-up programmes, rapid response teams, expanded multi-systemic therapy, and stronger co-operation between police and child welfare services. At the same time, swift, targeted and age-appropriate responses are needed when children commit serious offences. Fast-track procedures are being expanded nationwide, capacity in youth correctional units is increasing and new care programmes for serious young offenders are being tested. Criminal organizers who exploit children must face severe consequences. Norway has introduced a new offense targeting those who involve minors in crime and launched major initiatives against criminal networks and human trafficking. Overall, Norway seeks a balanced approach that combines effective prevention with proportional sanctions and encourages all countries to carefully consider this balance when responding to child offenders. President, community trust and resilience are essential to preventing and combating crime. Accountable public institutions, independent media, and an active civil society are vital pillars of resilient societies. Effective crime prevention and criminal justice policies must be human rights-based, gender-responsive, and inclusive. We welcome the Abu Dhabi Declaration, which reaffirms and advances our shared commitment to international cooperation in crime prevention and criminal justice. As we move forward, we should strive to strengthen the effectiveness, implementation and coherence of the conventions and other instruments at our disposal, ensuring that they remain fit for purpose in a rapidly changing world. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you very much, Your Excellency, for your statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Jorge Augustine Molina Arambury, Ambassador of Argentina in the United Arab Emirates. Excellency, you have the floor.

President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, First of all, allow me on behalf of the Argentine Republic to convey our sincere gratitude to the United Arab Emirates for the excellent organization of this Congress and for the warm welcome that has been provided. President, my country welcomes the adoption of the Abu Dhabi Declaration, which will guide the work of the international community in the area of crime prevention and criminal justice for the next five years. Today, transnational organized crime poses one of the greatest threats to the security of states, affecting the political, socioeconomic, and cultural development of our peoples. It is a multifaceted phenomenon which takes the form of trafficking in persons, drugs trafficking, corruption, smuggling of migrants, and of firearms and money laundering, inter alia. In addition, there are new modalities that harness emerging technologies and digital environments. These threats do not recognize borders, neither physical nor digital borders, and no state can tackle them on its own. Argentina is convinced that the only way to prevail and to effectively combat these new criminal modalities is by strengthening international cooperation. President, the Argentine Republic is party to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and its protocols, and participated actively in the process that led to its adoption. We believe that this serves as a reference legal framework in order to prevent and combat this phenomenon, and that all actions in this area must be undertaken in full respect for international law and the sovereignty of states. In this regard, we participated in the review mechanism of the Convention, both in our capacity as a reviewed state as well as a reviewing state. Furthermore, Our country has ample experience in terms of international legal cooperation in criminal matters, drawing on an extensive network of instruments. And based on that practical experience, we wish to underscore the central role of the central authorities as a link among national authorities, and as a area where efforts should be pooled in order to ensure more nimble mutual legal assistance and extradition. President, Argentina's commitment is equally reflected in our active participation in various multilateral and regional fora. When it comes to anti-money laundering actions and preventing financing of terrorism, Argentina has completed its fourth peer review within the International Financial Action Task Force, with results that reflect the progress that has been made in terms of technical compliance and effectiveness. We condemn all forms and manifestations of the prevention of the recruitment and exploitation of children and youth by criminal groups and terrorists, and particularly welcome the emphasis in the declaration that is placed on preventing the recruitment and exploitation of children and youth by criminal and terrorist groups. Within the Organization of American States, Argentina is currently exercising the chair of the expert group on anti-money laundering, as well as chairing the Meeting of National Authorities on Transnational Organized Crime, which will convene its next session in November 2026. Furthermore, we recognize the Police Community of the Americas, AMERIPOL, as a regional benchmark for police cooperation to tackle transnational organized crime and emerging crimes. President, Argentina's priorities focus on the unrestricted defense of life, freedom, and individual rights. This requires a victim-centered approach, as well as victim repairs. in addition to effective justice systems that are able to provide an agile response to new challenges and to prosecute and sanction crimes. Argentina sustains its staunch commitment to the instruments of the United Nations and the work of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. And we repeat our readiness to continue working towards building safer, more just societies, based on our understanding that crime prevention and strengthening the rule of law are indispensable pillars for development and also a shared responsibility for the international community.
I now give the floor to Mr. Oleksandr Balanusta, Ambassador of Ukraine to the United Arab Emirates. Excellency, the floor is yours.

Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, distinguished guests,

I would like to thank the UAE for your warm hospitality. Thank you very much.

Expressing our sincere appreciation to the United Arab Emirates for their very warm hospitality and excellent organization of this Congress. For Ukraine, the issues discussed by the Congress are not abstract. Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine has fundamentally changed our security environment and created new and highly complex challenges for the law enforcement, criminal justice, and crime prevention. At the same time, it has demonstrated the significance of strong institutions, international cooperation, and rule of law. In this context, I would like to highlight the importance that Ukraine attaches to the partnership in the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. Our cooperation with UNODC has become increasingly practical and comprehensive. It covers criminal justice reform, combating organized crime, corruption, trafficking, firearms control, prison reform, border management, other areas critical to Ukraine's security and recovery. We particularly value the fact that UNODC has remained present in Ukraine throughout the war. This presence matters. It means that UNODC is not only providing expertise from a distance, but is working with Ukrainian institutions on ground, understanding our changing needs, and helping us develop sustainable national capacities. We also highly appreciate the visit to Ukraine by Ms. Monica Njuma, Executive Director of UNODC, and Director General of the UNOV last August on the occasion of the 31st restoration of independence of Ukraine. This was a particularly meaningful gesture of solidarity and partnership. The visit demonstrated that the UNODC remains committed to Ukraine and is ready to further deepen our practical cooperation. We're grateful to Ms. Juna for her engagements with Ukrainian authorities and institutions for their clear focus on strengthening the partnership in this year's -- in this year's ahead. One of the areas we see significant potential is addressing criminal and security challenges resulting from the Russians' war. This includes organized crime, trafficking, illicit firearms flows, border and cargo security, emerging forms of cyber-enabled and technology-facilitated crimes. Of particular importance is maritime security. Ukraine's maritime corridor has become a critical element of global food security and international trade. The security of Ukrainian ports, vessels, legitimate route is therefore not only national issues, but also a matter of international cooperation. UNODC expertise and practical programs in maritime crime, passenger and cargo control can make an important contribution in this area. Looking ahead, Ukraine has high expectations for the next five-year period of cooperation with UNODC. We attach particular importance to the development of the UNODC Strategic Country Vision for Ukraine. We see this process as an important opportunity to jointly define the priorities and areas of cooperation that will guide our partnership throughout many years to come. We hope that this new strategic country vision will reflect Ukraine's evolving needs and the new war-related challenges, while providing a strong framework for practical, targeted, and result-oriented cooperation. Against the backdrop of attempts to frame international legal cooperation as a matter of politicization, Ukraine stresses that the focus of this Congress must remain on strengthening practical and effective cooperation in crime prevention and criminal justice. For Ukraine, such cooperation is essential to strengthening law enforcement institution, criminal justice, counteracting organized crime, corruption, trafficking, illicit firearms, border and cargo control, as I mentioned, including the maritime domain, supporting prison reform, building capacities to address new and emerging forms of crime. The concept of depoliticization must not be invoked to question legitimate international cooperation, obstruct accountability, or undermine the rule of law. International legal cooperation must remain firmly grounded on international law, due process, and shared responsibility to prevent crime, ensure justice, and combat impunity. In this context, Ukraine sees significant value in strengthening UNODC operational engagement in Ukraine and expanding technical assistance, capacity building, institutional cooperation with Ukrainian counterparts. We are not only a recipient of international assistance. Ukraine has accumulated substantial practical experience in confronting new forms of transnational crime under the extraordinary conditions created by the war. We believe that this experience can contribute to the work of UNODC and have broader international discussion on crime prevention. Mr. President, Ukraine highly values its partnership with UNODC. We look forward to working closely with Executive Director Monica Juma and her team in developing the strategic country vision and translating into concrete projects and practical results. We are confident that coming five years can become a period of even stronger, more structured, more result-oriented cooperation between Ukraine and UNDC. Ukraine stands ready to contribute actively to this partnership. Thank you very much. And once again, thank you for the United Arab Emirates for hosting us.
Thank you very much, Your Excellency. I now give the floor to Her Excellency, Ms. Nulenoji Alix Minister of Justice of Chad. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, President. Distinguished Executive Director of UNODC, Director General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. The Republic of Chad is pleased to participate in this 15th United Nations Crime Congress. We reiterate our commitment to the principles of the rule of law, human rights, fair access to justice, and enhancing international cooperation in preventing and combating crime. This comes at a time where organized crime has multiple forms and manifestations, such as transnational organized crime, terrorism, trafficking in persons, smuggling of migrants, cybercrime, laundering of money, corruption, drug trafficking, and crimes using ICT. Preventing organized crime for our country is a priority. It has to be seen through a global approach, bringing together public institutions, the judiciary, security forces, communities, civil society, women, youth, academia, and international partners. There must be public policies designed, emphasizing social unity, education, social inclusion, as well as employment, and combating inequalities and protecting vulnerable persons. We have resolutely committed to combating corruption and economic and financial crime. To these ends, we've established institutions and adapted our legal framework, as well as created mechanisms for prevention, oversight of investigation, and judicial cooperation. Digital transformation has offered new avenues for organized crime and online scams, but also in particular for the sexual exploitation of children online. This is an ongoing threat to our states. which goes beyond borders. For us, combating ICT crime is urgent and is a matter of protecting most vulnerable persons. We call for appropriate protection and a strategy that sees our legislations, institutions, and purviews keeping step with the changing nature of crime while upholding fundamental freedoms. Transnational organized crime is constantly changing, and no state can act alone. Criminal groups and terrorist groups manipulate borders and new technologies. We are pushing back against them without mercy and call for an enhancement of judicial cooperation, MLA, extradition, and joint investigation for transfer of sentenced persons and information exchange. These are key tools for us to use collectively. Our participation here is a time to reiterate these views and something which should be largely shared, namely that preventing crime and ensuring criminal justice are shared responsibilities. The blight of current organized crime and its remedy requires showing of cooperation and sharing experience. This cannot be done by an isolated region or state or institution. It is along these lines that today we seek to make our political commitment a specific commitment through Pledge for Justice. On behalf of the Government of the Republic of Chad, I am pleased to announce, so as to progress in preventing crime and ensuring criminal justice, the Republic of Chad commits, between 2026 to 2031, to strengthen national coordination in crime prevention and criminal justice, improve access to justice and the protection of most vulnerable persons, and strengthening regional and international judiciary cooperation, in particular when it comes to mutual legal assistance, extradition and transfer of sentenced persons. Through this, we will, in particular, bolster cooperation between our institutions and improve people's access to justice, while paying particular attention to vulnerable persons. In addition, to strengthening national mechanisms for prevention, victim protection and prosecution of perpetrators. We would also like to enhance prevention at a community level while acknowledging the role that women and youth and traditional authorities and community leaders can play here as well as civil society. We have a very clear goal, making justice a more accessible, effective and prevention and protection-based instrument. We believe that all of this depends on the quality of our partnerships. We will thus work with the United Nations and in particular the UNODC, African Union, regional organizations, state partners, civil society, academia, and technical and financial partners so as to ensure that this commitment leads to specific outcomes. Ladies and gentlemen, Pledge for Justice is not just words. For us, it is a political commitment which will pave the way for a national process for implementation, follow-up assessment, and will bear fruit up until 2031. It will strengthen the rule of law, human justice and security, and international cooperation in light of shared challenges. We support the Abu Dhabi Declaration, and as such, will work with all of our partners to enhance the prevention of crime and criminal justice, which should be accessible, have a human face, and to guarantee the protection of persons and the upholding of their rights, as well as offer prospects for social reintegration. We thank the host country for the organization of this Congress. It is our hope that this will be a time to shore up our collective action, in particular give way to collective responses in line with challenges facing us. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Thank you very much to her Excellency for that statement and commitment and pledge. Thank you.

Excellency, Ms. Arusha Vinodini Coore, Ambassador and Permanent Representative of Sri Lanka. Sorry for that. I now give the floor to Mr. Abbas Bagherpoor, Director General for Legal and International Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to begin by appreciating the tremendous efforts made by UAE for the organization of the 15th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice. An effective and accountable criminal justice system is indispensable to preventing crime, ensuring justice, protecting rights, and maintaining public confidence in the administration of justice. Mr. President, we gather at a time when the world is advancing toward digitalization at an unprecedented pace. In an era of rapid technological change, artificial intelligence has emerged as an innovative tool that can significantly enhance crime prevention strategies, provided that its use remains responsible, transparent, and human-centered, and can strengthen the capacity of states to prevent crime, protect victims, and promote public safety, while expanding access to justice and legal awareness. However, while emerging technologies have opened new horizons for development, they have simultaneously placed sophisticated tools in the hands of criminals and terrorists, even including the tools that challenge geographical borders, national sovereignty, and territorial integrity of other states. In fact, we face a sustained pattern of threats aggression, and contempt for the most basic rules of international law. And all of those have been accompanied by including an aspect of using new technologies. Cyber attacks against wider infrastructure, hacking banking systems, using social media to disseminate misinformation and disinformation, issuing rewards for revealing the whereabouts of officials, and recruiting terrorists are among crimes enabled by cyber technologies. As an alarming case in point, during the acts of aggression committed since February, in clear breach of the basic principles of international law, facilitated through the use of territory of other states, everything, including these technologies, have been used for commission of war crimes against the Iranian nation. This is why we believe that technology must be harnessed for the cause of justice, not for the perpetration of crime. Mr. President, attaching great importance to strengthening crime prevention and criminal justice, the Islamic Republic of Iran has taken concrete steps, including its accession to the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crimes and its signing of the UN Convention against Cybercrime. Iran has also developed its legislative, judicial, and administrative frameworks to combat various forms of crime. Moreover, Iran, at the forefront of combating terrorism, has continued its effort to prevent and counter terrorism at regional and international level. In addition, Iran has undertaken a range of crime prevention initiatives aimed at raising public awareness and improving access to justice. Only through the National Judge at the School Program, approximately 275,000 students, parents, and educators have received legal and judicial training, contributing to a more inclusive, accessible, and people-centered criminal justice system. Mr. President, endeavors in crime prevention, criminal justice, and the rule of law being the very theme of this meeting, should promote international cooperation towards a world free from crime. Addressing and countering crime, including organized crime and terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, is impossible. It's impossible without international cooperation. However, unilateral coercive measures, UCMs, imposing contravention of international law and the UN Charter, continue to impede such cooperation. These measures obstruct access to essential equipment, technologies, and financial resources required for the effective criminal justice responses. A glaring example of such unlawful measures is the campaign currently being waged against Iran, which is using economic coercion as an alternative instrument of the failed act of aggression, seeking to pursue the same objectives by systematically targeting Iranian population under new, but another failed attempt announced in August 2026. The aggressor is now weaponizing economic deprivation as an instrument of collective punishment and political coercion, directly violating the fundamental rights of not only Iranian people, but also other nations. This is why we continue to highlight this matter as a serious obstacle in the field of international cooperation in crime prevention and criminal justice. In fact, in the light of the current global circumstances, this matter has assumed even greater significance. And needless to highlight that, to that end, respect for all human rights, including the right to development, is a must, and collective efforts to realize it are required. To conclude, Mr. President, the Islamic Republic of Iran and its understanding of these evolving challenges, we affirm its readiness to work in constructively to strengthen international cooperation in preventing and combating crime and promote a world that upholds every member to the same kind of standards. In this regard, we look forward to a productive deliberation during this session. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you very much, Your Excellency. I now give the floor to the United Nations African Institute for Ms. Robina Nakibuka, Prevention of Crime and Treatment of Finance and Administrative Assistant Offenders.

Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. We extend our sincere appreciation to the United Arab Emirates for its gracious hospitality and for hosting this 15th United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice. UNAFRI fully aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group and embraces the urgent purpose of this 15th United Nations Congress. Dear delegates, crime does not respect borders, and neither can our response. Across Africa, terrorism and violent extremism, trafficking in persons and firearms, kidnappings, cybercrime, corruption, financial and economic crimes are increasingly prevalent and more interconnected than ever before. Criminal networks exploit technology, weak coordination, and vulnerable communities, especially women and young children. Our response is therefore, dear delegates, must be coordinated, innovative, and people-centered. UNAFRI has supported African states in developing effective crime prevention policies, strengthening the criminal justice systems, and promoting rehabilitation and deepening regional and international cooperation. Our strategic plan for 2024-2028 renews that purpose and aligns our work with Sustainable Development Goal 16 and the aspirations of African Union Agenda 2063. Since the Kyoto Congress, INAFRI has convened and supported engagements on human trafficking, first responders and scene of crime management, access to justice and legal aid, digital assets and efficient intelligence, cybercrime and prison reform, anti-corruption, rehabilitation and integration of offenders, and the protection of women, children, and other vulnerable groups. We are also strengthening frontline capacity through practical training for law enforcement and justice officials to identify crime indicators, protect victims, investigate effectively, preserve evidence, pursue criminal networks, and support successful prosecutions. Stronger skills at every stage strengthen the entire justice chain. We are building an African Crime Data Center ACDC, and calling on partners to join us in that endeavor and to always give us data when we call upon you. Our other priority is to extend prevention beyond institutions and into the communities. Through the African Youth Crime Prevention Platform and other digital channels, UNIFRA is convening young Africans, experts, practitioners, policymakers, and the public to address trafficking, cyber crime, fraud, drug use, mob justice, xenophobia, prisoners' rights, and rehabilitation. We carried some of our literature on what the youth, African youth, are saying, and we've been passing it around. Young people must not be treated only as beneficiaries of peace and security. They must be recognized as partners, innovators, and leaders in preventing crime. Giving them knowledge, platforms and opportunity is an investment in safer communities and a safer continent. Our other priority is to expand partnerships with the UNODC, the Programme Network of Institutes, the International Criminal Court, universities, human rights bodies, civil society and youth organizations to advance research, training and rehabilitation. Accountability and knowledge exchange. Africa must not only be a recipient of global criminal justice knowledge, but also must help shape global solutions to these problems. Excellencies, UNAFRI has a distinctive place in Africa's security and justice architecture. We therefore call upon African states that have not yet signed or acceded to the UNAFRI statute to consider doing so. Wider membership will strengthen our cooperation as Africa, will strengthen research, training, and the exchange of African solutions to African and global challenges. As I conclude, we express our sincere appreciation to the United Nations for its continued support to the Institute and to African governments for honoring their assessed financial contributions to the Institute. Excellencies, We express our profound appreciation to every member state in Africa, partner and practitioner, whose commitment sustains our shared mission. We thank the government of Uganda that hosts this institute and that has given us very generous facilities in which we operate. We also appeal to you as this Congress to stand with UNAIFRI with renewed political will, stronger partnerships, and the resources needed to translate our collective resolve into lasting action. A safer Africa is possible. A more just Africa is possible. A peaceful Africa is possible. And an Africa in which young people are at the center of crime prevention is possible. Together, let us build Africa. Thank you very much.
